extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_short: examining Markush groupings and prior art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating propriety of Markush groupings (35 U.S.C. 112 issues) and for choosing and using prior art (35 U.S.C. 102/103) during patent examination. Covers standards, examples, and procedural steps examiners should follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush grouping (written description) — 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should not suggest a grouping that meets the requirements for a proper Markush grouping, but would clearly lack adequate written description if presented in a separate claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject claims based on an improper Markush grouping under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) when the grouping would not meet written description requirements if recited in separate claims. Maintain the improper Markush grouping rejection until the claim is amended to correct the grouping or the applicant convinces the examiner that the members share the required similarity and common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness of Markush claim — 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) if one skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the Markush claim due to an inability to envision all of the members of the Markush grouping. If a boundary cannot be drawn separating embodiments encompassed by the claim from those that are not, the claim is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness) when the Markush grouping prevents a person of ordinary skill from drawing clear boundaries. See also MPEP § 2173.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine other patentability conditions despite Markush issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be examined for patentability with respect to all other conditions of patentability (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, 112, and nonstatutory double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when issuing an improper Markush grouping rejection, continue to evaluate claims for other statutory and nonstatutory grounds. Per MPEP § 803.02, search need not be extended to species that fall outside a proper Markush grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to withdraw improper Markush grouping rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The improper Markush grouping rejection should be maintained until (1) the claim is amended such that the Markush grouping includes only members that share a single structural similarity and a common use; or (2) the applicant presents convincing arguments why the members of the Markush grouping share a single structural similarity and common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convincing arguments may show that alternatives are members of a physical, chemical, or art-recognized class that share a common use, or that chemical compounds share a substantial structural feature essential to the common use. Reconsider the rejection when all claims are otherwise in condition for allowance and the prior art and record support propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush grouping is decided case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of Markush groupings must be decided on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent examples as illustrative only; evaluate the facts of each claim and class of compounds (or alternatives) individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider compounds as wholes (Harnisch / In re Jones principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the propriety of a Markush grouping the compounds must be considered as wholes and not broken down into elements or other components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing structural similarity and common use, focus on commonality across all alternative embodiments rather than on isolated substituent moieties defined by the Markush terminology. See In re Harnisch and In re Jones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-prong test for propriety of chemical Markush groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is proper if the members share (1) a substantial single structural similarity and (2) a common use (utility) that flows from that structural feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical compounds evaluate each claimed compound as a whole to determine whether both prongs are met. The common use should be tied to the substantial structural feature disclosed as essential to that utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient common structural proportion (prong 1 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed class shows a relatively large proportion of the structure common to the entire class, the prong 1 requirement for structural similarity may be met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a substantial portion of the molecules' structure is shared across the class (example: common coumarin core or phosphoric acid diester backbone). Breadth due to indices (e.g., repeating units) does not automatically defeat prong 1 if the common structure is substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common use requirement (prong 2 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: All of the compounds must share a common disclosed use (e.g., being dyes, antimycotic activity) and that use should be related to the substantial structural feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the disclosed utility is common to the claimed members and flows from the shared structural feature; mere potential multiple modes of application does not preclude a finding of common use if the compounds form a single invention/subgenus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush when alternatives are from disparate classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is improper if the alternatives are not all members of the same recognized physical or chemical class or the same art-recognized class, nor do they share both a substantial structural feature and a common use that flows from that feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify if alternatives represent multiple chemical classes with varying structures (e.g., inorganic salts, organic acids, amides, nitriles, phenols, amines, heterocyclics). If so, the grouping likely fails. Use prior art and technical knowledge about incompatibilities or differing activities to support the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of prior art — confine rejections to best available art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are permitted (for claim-interpretation dependence, missing inventive concept, AIA-specific exceptions, or pre-AIA §102(e)/(f)/(g) qualification). Provide best backup rejections where appropriate, avoid merely cumulative rejections, and back up rejections with the best other art available to allow compact prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on abstracts vs underlying foreign-language documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When both the abstract and the underlying document qualify as prior art, the underlying document should normally be used to support a rejection. When an abstract is used, the evidence relied upon is the facts contained in the abstract, not additional facts in the underlying full text document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and analyze the underlying document; if non-English, obtain a translation so the record is clear. An abstract can have a different effective publication date than the full text. In limited circumstances an examiner may rely on an abstract alone in a non-final action but should supply the full text and translation in the next action. See Ex parte Jones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of machine translation for foreign documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on a machine translation of a foreign language document unless the machine translation is not of sufficient quality to be adequate evidence of the contents of the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant provides evidence (e.g., a translation inconsistent with the machine translation) showing the machine translation does not accurately represent the document’s contents, the examiner should obtain a human translation. Office actions supplying full text or translations may be made final only under specified conditions (see MPEP §§706.07).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or implicitly (inherent). For a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection, the reference teachings must be modified in a way that would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 102 where a single reference discloses all claim limitations; apply 103 where combinations or modifications of references would have been obvious. See MPEP §§2131–2146 and §§2150–2159.04 for detailed guidance on 102/103 determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine effective filing date and reference date for applying 102
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine which paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 102 applies, the effective filing date of the application and each claimed invention must be determined and compared with the date of the reference. The examiner must also determine the issue or publication date of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate MPEP sections (e.g., §§2139.01, 2152.01, 2124, 2126, 2128–2128.02, 2152.02–2154.02(c)) to determine dates. Use form paragraphs 7.03.aia or 7.03.fti in Office actions to indicate AIA vs pre-AIA status and which 102 paragraph applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection by (i) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art, or (ii) amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art. Additional ways depend on whether claims are subject to AIA provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2152.06 for overcoming 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) rejections and MPEP §§2132.01, 2133.02(a), 2136.05 et seq. for pre-AIA strategies. Consider invoking exceptions (e.g., 37 CFR 1.130 or 1.131 affidavits/declarations) or demonstrating common ownership/joint research agreements where applicable.
